Text.Text: You're in my incident file under resolution. First time I've written that word since I took this office. The lower yard holds, the lockdown is lifted, and I still don't trust you - but it's professional courtesy now, not suspicion. Carry it well.

Stop there. You've passed my checkpoint twice this week, and I file patterns. You're not cleared for what's below, and your hands say your katar work still has teachers left in it. When there is nothing left for anyone to show you, we talk. Until then you're a civilian, and civilians stay above deck.

Where were you when the lower yard went into lockdown? Don't answer - I already pulled the records. You were off-station, which makes you the only katar hand on CZ-220 I can't place inside the breach. That makes you useful. A crew sealed the CZ-220 Breaker Yard's lower level and they're running katar drills behind my own containment doors. Six adepts hold the outer bays under a work order my office never issued. Put all six down and bring me the Scrapheap Lockdown Breaker Yard Work Order. The flimsi is forged, and forgeries name their forgers.

No codes. A key - physical, logged to you, and if it walks I know exactly who walked it. The way down is the containment door my own board insists doesn't exist anymore. Six adepts. One flimsi. Anything else you touch down there ends up in my report, so touch carefully.

From the inside. Lockdown protocol seals trouble in - it should never seal me out. Someone rewrote the sequence so my override reads as the intrusion. My own doors treat me as the breach. That isn't a hack, it's authorship. Only a few people alive understand the protocol well enough to turn it inside out, and I wrote most of that list myself.

Katar containment work. Lockdown doctrine - you don't chase the fight, you close the room around it until nothing inside moves without your permission. Done right, it's the cleanest discipline I ever cleared a permit for. Done down there, off the books, behind my own doors, it's a weapon program with this yard's name on the liability line.

On its own, nothing - paper is paper. But a forgery is a confession with a signature. Stamp codes, routing marks, the requisition chain: every line tells me who inside my perimeter fed them formats, schedules, and door timings. I don't need it to convict the six you're about to meet. I need it for the ones you won't.
The outer bays are still theirs and my evidence is still on the wrong side of a containment door. Six adepts. One work order. Report back.
You came up the south lift eight minutes faster than your last exit, and your hand hasn't left your pack since you stepped off it. That's evidence you're carrying. The work order. Now.

Routing marks. Requisition chain. There. He taps the flimsi once. "This format revision was retired years before you ever docked here. Whoever fed it to them worked this office back then. That's a shorter list than I feared and a longer one than I like. Payment's logged. You're still a suspect - but you're my suspect now."

Second incident. While you were clearing the outer bays, their specialists pulled the junkline control relay and wired it into a stand-off grid of their own design. Every belt down there is a wall that moves now. Five specialists run the grid in rotation - I've timed them through the door sensors. Break the rotation, put all five down, and recover the Scrapheap Lockdown Junkline Control Relay. Without it, their lockdown starts eating its own power.

The reroute hub is north along the junkline. You'll hear it before you see it - belts running against their own load rating. The five keep a two-on watch, and they are better than the adepts you filed away. Assume everything I tell you is understatement. It usually is.

An engineered one. Every bay is rigged against every other bay - belts, gates, pressure doors, cross-wired so touching one wakes three. My response protocols assume a threat that wants out. This crew wants to stay in. Holding sealed ground is the whole doctrine they're drilling. The stand-off isn't their defense. It's their thesis.

Two things. It's the switch their moving walls hang from - pull it and their perimeter goes from active to static, which is the difference between fighting a machine and fighting furniture. And it's serial-logged. The maintenance record will show me when it was accessed and under whose credentials. Hardware doesn't lie. That's why I prefer it to people.

Regulation. My teams deploy three-strong or not at all - I enforce that rule, and I've buried the exceptions to it. Right now every three-man cell I trust is holding the upper yard so this stays contained to one deck. You're what I have left that fights like three. When you go below the sheared bay line, that regulation applies to you as well. Remember that I said so.
Their walls still move. Five specialists at the reroute hub, one relay. My board goes quiet the moment you pull it, so I'll know before you do.

My board went static forty minutes ago. Their grid is furniture now, which means my relay is in your pack. That burn on your forearm is junkline voltage - don't clean it with yard water. The relay. Here.

Already checking the access log. He reads the maintenance record, and something in his jaw sets. "Retired credentials. Same era as the forged format. I know who trained this crew. I think I've known since the first door sealed on me. Payment's logged. Keep the key. This incident file just grew a name I'm not ready to say out loud."

New classification: containment failure. Their warden has fortified the sheared bay, the deepest sealed section, and every probe I send past his line stops existing. He wears the bay's sigil plate as authorization - as long as it hangs on him, the old dock systems read his lockdown as legitimate. Kill the warden and take the Scrapheap Lockdown Sheared Bay Sigil, and their authority down there dies with him. Regulation applies: you go three-strong or you don't go. That's not advice. That's the section of the protocol written in other people's blood.

Names. Give me the names of your two before you go - if this goes wrong I want three accurate lines in the casualty report, not guesses. He writes, then looks up. "The sheared bay is past the reroute hub, at the bottom of the junkline. He'll let all three of you in. Wardens like him don't stop entries. They stop exits."

Nothing, which tells me everything. Every feed dies at the same threshold - not jammed, ended. The last frame probe six sent was him standing in the exact center of the bay, arms down, waiting. Fourteen hours later, probe seven sent the same frame. He doesn't patrol. He doesn't sleep where I can measure it. He is the lockdown.

Commissioning law. The oldest docks on this station predate my office, and their emergency systems answer to bay sigils - physical authority, no network to subvert. Whoever wears the sheared bay's plate is the sheared bay, as far as the old machinery cares. Elegant. Also the single point of failure in their entire occupation, hung on the one man they're certain can't be taken. I'm paying you to audit that assumption.

No. Not yet. I give you a name, you carry it down there, and a name changes how you fight - you start looking for a face instead of an opening. I'll say this much: the lockdown below wasn't subverted. It is running exactly as designed, by the man who designed it. Deal with the warden first. The rest of that sentence is waiting at the bottom of the yard.
The warden still holds the sheared bay and my probes still die at his line. Three of you. One of him. Those still aren't good odds, so stop standing here.
Probe eight crossed the threshold this morning and came back. First one in two quarters. There's a body in the center frame and a bare hook where a sigil plate used to hang. Give it to me.

Then the old docks answer to this office again. He hangs the plate on the board behind him, dead center. "Casualty report reads: none, ours. I have filed a great deal of paper against that man's line, and this is the first page that says we crossed it. Hazard rate for all three of you - tell your two to collect in person. I want faces for the names I didn't have to file."

This one is a conspiracy charge. Four remain of the crew's inner circle, and between them they hold the foreman's override chip - the master key to every containment system on the lower decks. My lockdown, their lockdown, anyone's: whoever holds that chip owns the concept. They know their warden is gone. They've stopped drilling and started fortifying, which means they've stopped being students and become accomplices. All four go down, and the Scrapheap Lockdown Foreman's Override Chip comes to me. Keep your two with you. This is still deep-yard work.

They hold the crane deck above the drill pit, and every gate on the way answers to the chip they carry - expect each door to be a decision they've already made. Don't try to out-lock lockdown students. Go through them. It's the one argument their doctrine respects.

The others were recruits. These four are believers. Each one can hold a sealed room alone until thirst wins - I've watched them drill exactly that on the feeds I still have. They eat facing the doors. They sleep in coverage arcs. And they have never once tripped one of my sensors by accident. If the man who trained them is who I believe, these four are his footnotes. Footnotes are where the dangerous details live.

Because my office runs on authorization, and that chip is authorization - physical, final, older than the network. Seated in the yardmaster's board, it's a tool. Loose, in doctrine-drilled hands, it's the power to declare any deck, dock, or corridor a sealed exercise, and every system I run would call it legal. Recover it, and their occupation goes back to being what it always was. Trespass.

Fine. You've earned the file. The man below wrote the lockdown protocol this station still runs. My predecessor. I inherited his office, his regulations, and his signature on half the standing orders I still enforce - three-strong deployment included. He resigned the week I was promoted, walked below decks, and I certified the report that said he left the station. The crew, the drills, the stand-off: his doctrine, taught by his own hand. When the circle falls, he is what's left, and I will be sending you down to correct my own paperwork.
Four believers on the crane deck, one override chip. Until it seats in my board, every sealed door on this station is arguing about who it works for.
Every gate on the lower decks reverted to my authority in the same second. That's not a malfunction. That's a chip coming loose from four dead grips. Let me see it.

Seated. Verified. Mine. The chip clicks into the yardmaster's board, and half the alarm lights he has lived under go dark. "The conspiracy charge closes at four counts. What's left below isn't a crew anymore - it's one man, one bay, and one conversation I've spent years not having. Collect your pay, then sleep. The last incident is the oldest one."

Final incident. The man who wrote the lockdown is all that's left below. He holds the deepest bay under the original protocol - his own, unrevised, the pure version he never let anyone file. I watch him through the one feed he permits me to keep, and you should understand what that means: he wants this. Everything you've fought down there was his doctrine secondhand. He is the doctrine, and the katar work you've bled to learn is his, finished. There's nothing to recover this time. He is the last item on the charge sheet, and the charge is everything. Take your two. No one has ever walked out of a room he decided to close - my three-strong regulation exists because of him, and it's the only part of his work I intend to keep.

The last door is at the bottom of everything - past the sheared bay, past the crane deck, the bay with no number. Your key will open it because he wants it to. Understand that going in: every door that opens for you down there is him accepting the appointment. Keep your two inside arm's reach, and do not let him choose the room.

Because the protocol was never about the yard. I've read his early drafts. Lockdown, the way he wrote it, is a promise: nothing gets past me. Not the fight, not the fear, not one thing he ever failed to contain. A man makes enough of those promises and eventually he builds a room shaped like himself and keeps the last promise from inside it. He didn't subvert my station. He finally filed himself where he always belonged.

The finished form of everything they drilled at you. The adepts held floors. The specialists held rooms. The warden held a line for two quarters against everything I could send. He taught all of them, and I hold exactly one recording of him working: a boarding raid, eleven years back, four raiders sealed in a cargo lock with him. The door cycled once. He walked out carrying the manifest they came for. That lock is still classified. Whatever your katars learned on the way down to him - it's his, and he will use it back at you without the copies' flaws.

Chief of security with a clean file, for the first time since I took the office. I certified a false report once - that he left this station - because it was easier than certifying what he had become. Every incident since is interest on that lie. When this is done I write the correction myself: full account, my signature, whatever it costs. He taught me that the paperwork has to hold even when nothing else does. Especially then.
He's still below, holding the pure protocol, and my charge sheet still has one open line. Three-strong. Go close it.
His feed went dark an hour ago. Then every containment door on the lower decks released - all of them, in the same breath, like the station exhaling. The protocol only lets go one way. Report.

Then the file is complete. First page to last, every charge resolved. He signs it slowly, and for once his eyes are not checking the corridor behind you. "You beat containment doctrine with the one thing it can't plan for - three people who trust each other inside a sealed room. He'd have called that the flaw in his protocol. I'm filing it as the fix. Your pay, at hazard rate, and my correction goes up the chain tonight. The lockdown below is lifted. Both of them are."
Back to the incident.
Sign out the key. I'll bring you the forgery.
How does a crew lock you out of your own protocol?
What kind of drills need a sealed deck?
What does one forged flimsi actually prove?
I don't take work from people mid-interrogation. Not today.
The Scrapheap Lockdown Breaker Yard Work Order. Six fewer people can explain it.
About the relay.
Five specialists. I'll break the rotation.
A stand-off made of belts. Explain that.
What does the relay give you?
Why not send your own response teams?
Time their rotation again. I'll be back for it.
The Scrapheap Lockdown Junkline Control Relay. Check the access log - your hardware doesn't lie.
Back to the warden.
Three-strong, then. I'll bring two I'd trust in a sealed room.
What did your lost probes tell you about him?
How does a plate on his chest command your systems?
You said you know who trained them. Say the name.
I only count two of us today. I'll return at three.
The Scrapheap Lockdown Sheared Bay Sigil. Your single point of failure, audited.
Back to the chip.
Four accomplices, one chip. Filed by morning.
What separates the circle from the rest?
Why does one chip outrank your entire office?
It's time. Tell me who is at the bottom of the yard.
Four dug-in believers takes planning. Keep the file open.
The Scrapheap Lockdown Foreman's Override Chip. Your conspiracy is down to one man.
Back to the last charge.
Then we close his room around him. All three of us.
Why does a man lock himself inside his own protocol?
What exactly am I walking into down there?
And when he's gone - what does that make you?
Not yet. When my three is certain, I'll go down.
It's closed. His lockdown ended with him.
